Amends an existing bayesmanecfit or bayesnecfit object

Source: R/amend.R
amend.Rd

Amends an existing bayesmanecfit or bayesnecfit object, for example, by adding or removing fitted models.

amend(
  object,
  drop,
  add,
  loo_controls,
  x_range = NULL,
  resolution = NULL,
  sig_val = NULL,
  priors,
  prior_type = NULL,
  asymptote_observed = NULL,
  timeout = Inf,
  predictor_scale = NULL
)

Arguments

object

An object of class bayesmanecfit or bayesnecfit, as returned by bnec.

drop

A character vector containing the names of model types you which to exclude for the modified fit. A bayesnecfit contains a single model, so there is nothing that can be dropped from it and drop is an error in that case.

add

A character vector containing the names of model types you which to include to the modified fit. Adding models to a bayesnecfit promotes it to a bayesmanecfit.

loo_controls

A named list of two elements, "fitting" and "weights", as for bnec. An element not named is taken from object: "fitting" holds the arguments object was built with, and "weights" holds them where they name the method its model weights were computed by. A "weights" list that names no method keeps that method.

x_range, resolution, sig_val

As for bnec. Each is taken from object unless supplied, and is the bnec default where object records none. The estimates of every model in the amended set are computed again with them, including the models already fitted. Supplying these arguments alone recomputes the estimates without refitting any model.

priors

An object of class brmsprior which specifies user-desired prior distributions of model parameters. It can also be specified as a named list where each name needs to correspond to the same string as model. Where it is not supplied, the prior of the call that fitted object is used as described in Details, and the default priors are built for each parameter it does not cover.

prior_type

A character string selecting the set of default priors to build for any newly added models, either "uninformative" or "regularizing". See bnec. Taken from object unless supplied, and "uninformative" where object records none.

asymptote_observed

A logical declaring whether the highest predictor level reached the lower asymptote, applied to the default priors and the initial-value search of any newly added models. See bnec. Taken from object unless supplied, and TRUE where object records none.

timeout

A positive numeric giving the maximum number of seconds allowed for fitting any single model, passed to withTimeout. This is useful when fitting multiple models, as it allows a model that is taking excessively long (for example because of highly divergent chains) to be abandoned so that the remaining models can still be fitted. A model that exceeds timeout is treated as a failed fit and dropped from the returned set. The default Inf imposes no limit. Requires the R.utils package to be installed when a finite value is supplied.

predictor_scale

A character string declaring whether the predictor is supplied as "concentration", already "log" transformed, or should use the "auto" rule, for the priors of any newly added models. See bnec. Taken from object unless supplied, and "auto" where object records none.

Value

All successfully fitted model fits. A bayesmanecfit if more than one model remains, otherwise a bayesnecfit.

Details

A model added through add is fitted with the arguments of the call that fitted object, read from its first model. It is sampled with that call's iter, warmup, thin, chains, sample_prior, backend, algorithm and save_pars, and any control or seed the call passed to brm. Its default priors are built with the call's prior_type, asymptote_observed and predictor_scale, unless those are supplied here. Other brm arguments, such as cores, are not passed to the added model, and neither is timeout.

Where priors is not supplied, an added model named in a list of priors given to bnec is given that model's element, as bnec would have given it. A single brmsprior given to bnec is not applied to an added model, because it names the parameters of the models it was written for, and a parameter of the same name can have a different role in another equation, as beta does. The added model is then given its default priors, and a message says so.

Where object has a two-block family, such as hurdle_gamma, the added model's survival block uses the equation the set was fitted with: the one model_survival named, or the added model's own equation where model_survival was not given.

Where object does not record its call, as an object fitted by an earlier version of bayesnec does not, no control, seed or prior is passed to the added model, its default priors are built with the bnec defaults of prior_type, asymptote_observed and predictor_scale, and the survival-block equation is read from the stored formulas. A single model whose survival block uses its own equation is then read as fitted without model_survival, because the two calls store the same formula. The estimates are computed with the bnec defaults of x_range, resolution, sig_val and loo_controls where object does not record those. update.bnecfit creates a call record for such an object, using the recovered survival-block equation and any control or seed supplied to the update. Subsequent additions reuse that record. amend also records the recovered equation on retained models, so dropping models does not discard it. When an update changes the backend or algorithm, brms does not reuse the previous control or seed. Only settings supplied to that update are then recorded for subsequent additions.

Examples

library(bayesnec)
data(manec_example)
exmp <- amend(manec_example, drop = "nec4param")
#> Only ecx4param is fitted, no model averaging done. Perhaps try setting better priors, or check ?show_params to make sure you have the correct parameter names for your priors.
#> Returning ecx4param
#> Warning: Found 5 observations with a pareto_k > 0.5 in model 'ecx4param'. We recommend to run more iterations to get at least about 2200 posterior draws to improve LOO-CV approximation accuracy.
#> Warning: 
#> 5 (5.0%) p_waic estimates greater than 0.4. We recommend trying loo instead.
